newsitem.title: UK: UK's new leader Blair forges ruling team.
newsitem.headline: UK's new leader Blair forges ruling team.

text.p: Prime Minister Tony Blair on Saturday carried out the promise he made after his landslide election victory to replace talking with action, completing the Labour party's first ruling cabinet in 18 years.

Blair, who will be 44 on Tuesday and is Britain's youngest prime minister in 185 years, included a record five women, giving a clear signal he intends to make a radical start to the government which will lead Britain into the next century.
He also named Britain's first openly homosexual minister, Chris Smith who became Heritage Secretary, and the first blind minister, Education and Employment Secretary David Blunkett.

Among the women, Marjorie "Mo" Mowlam -- a pugnacious politician who has just had treatment for a benign brain tumour -- was named Northern Ireland secretary and flew straight to Belfast for a walkabout and her first political meetings.
She faces a tough task to rescue a stalled process to bring peace to the British-ruled province and find a solution to a sectarian conflict rooted in history and steeped in blood.

Outspoken leftwinger Clare Short, tipped for exclusion after loose talk on taxes and legalising cannabis during the long election campaign, was rewarded with a seat at the Cabinet table as Secretary for International Development.

But the Conservatives, already reeling after their defeat which left them with the smallest number of members of parliament since 1906, were dealt a new blow when former deputy prime minister Michael Heseltine was taken to hospital.
Heseltine, who suffered a mild heart attack in 1993, was taken to hospital after suffering "mild angina pains".
Conservative headquarters said Heseltine had also confirmed he would not be a candidate for the party leadership to replace John Major, who has already said he is standing down.

The departure of Heseltine, favourite to take the job as a caretaker candidate, could turn the leadership battle into a bitter struggle for the heart of the party even before it has recovered from its deep electoral wounds.

But Blair's announcement of his cabinet appointments -- which carefully balanced right and left-wingers in the party he has radically overhauled to make it fit to rule -- showed a sure touch on the tiller despite his lack of government experience.
Other women named include Trade Secretary Margaret Beckett, Social Security Secretary Harriet Harman and Ann Taylor as leader of the House of Commons (lower house), a key parliamentary job.
The sober reality of government contrasted with the euphoria which greeted Blair's victory in Thursday's election.
Crowds dizzy with joy at Labour's biggest election victory cheered and sang as Blair arrived at 10 Downing Street, the prime ministerial residence, on Friday with his family.
On Saturday, Blair's young family -- his daughter Kathryn is nine and his sons Nicky and Euan, 11 and 13 respectively -- began grappling with the problem of where they will now live.
Aides said Blair and his wife, Cherie, had ruled out living above the Downing Street office because the apartment used by John Major and prime ministers before him was too small.
They now are looking at the larger flat next door, above the house that is traditionally occupied by the Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister).

Cherie, a successful lawyer who sacrificed her own political ambitions for her husband and who is likely to continue with her career, arrived at Downing Street at lunchtime on Saturday saying she was just getting used to the change in her life.
But the day did not start so well for the publicity-shy Cherie. She was caught on camera opening the door of her London home clad in a nightdress, hair ruffled and without make-up.
The expression on her face as she realised she was greeting not just the milkman but the world's press turned rapidly from surprise to horror as she beat a hurried retreat back inside.
